nodes.title: Global Finance and Trade Architecture
nodes.subtitle: Uneven Integration, Multilateral Institutions, and Systemic Financial Fragility
bullets: Postwar economic order established at Bretton Woods expanded global transactions unevenly across regions
Financial deregulation detached from regulatory control regimes generated systemic crisis and forced public bailouts

nodes.title: Act I: The Global Economy Puzzle
nodes.subtitle: Uneven Expansion, Flow Dynamics, and Regional Clustering
bullets: World trade expanded dramatically since 1970 but remained clustered in advanced industrial economies
Contrasts transaction intensity against geographic extensity and regional agreements against global integration

nodes.title: Dimensions of Global Economic Flows
nodes.subtitle: Analytical metrics distinguishing transaction magnitude from geographic reach
bullets: Disaggregates global interconnectedness into distinct density and dispersion dimensions
Framework essential for identifying whether globalization is truly worldwide or geographically narrow

nodes.title: Intensity of Economic Flows
nodes.subtitle: Magnitude and density of cross-border transactions across national borders
bullets: Measures trade volume, foreign direct investment, capital transfers, and migration density
Reflects deepening transaction frequency among heavily integrated industrial trading partners

nodes.title: Extensity of Economic Flows
nodes.subtitle: Geographical spread and worldwide reach of economic transactions across nations
bullets: Measures number of participating countries and global dispersion of cross-border linkages
Reveals whether economic networks encompass developing nations or remain spatially restricted

nodes.title: Spatial Organization of World Trade
nodes.subtitle: Contrasting worldwide economic integration against concentrated regional blocs
bullets: Examines whether trade growth represents genuine global inclusion or regional concentration
Identifies structural exclusion of peripheral developing nations from core trading circuits

nodes.title: Worldwide Economic Globalization
nodes.subtitle: Universal integration of economies across goods, capital, and technology
bullets: Theoretically envisions worldwide economic interdependence and reciprocal cross-border market opening
Promised comprehensive integration of developing economies into expanding global production networks

nodes.title: Regional Economic Integration
nodes.subtitle: Trade and investment flows clustered predominantly within regional trading blocs
bullets: FDI and goods commerce concentrate heavily inside North America, the European Union, and East Asia
Postwar trade growth driven by regional neighbor agreements rather than genuine worldwide inclusion

nodes.title: Geographically Uneven Globalization
nodes.subtitle: Persistent exclusion of peripheral economies from global trade benefits
bullets: Advanced industrial regions capture major trade gains while vast areas participate only marginally
Least developed countries operate on systemic margins with restricted market access and investment

nodes.title: Act II: Postwar Institutional Architecture
nodes.subtitle: Bretton Woods Foundations, Trade Evolution, and Governance Deficits
bullets: 1944 conference established multilateral framework to secure postwar monetary and trade stability
Evolution from GATT to WTO and lender voting inequality created structural developmental imbalances

nodes.title: Multilateral Trade Order
nodes.subtitle: Evolution from provisional GATT tariff rounds to binding WTO dispute resolution
bullets: Institutional transition designed to overcome negotiating bottlenecks and establish commerce rules
Confronts persistent deadlocks over developed country agricultural protectionism

nodes.title: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)
nodes.subtitle: 1947 provisional trade agreement reducing tariffs via unanimous consensus
bullets: Established rules and negotiating rounds for reducing tariffs and import quotas between nations
Unwieldy consensus structure required unanimous member agreement, leading to institutional gridlock

nodes.title: World Trade Organization (WTO)
nodes.subtitle: 1995 formal trade body establishing binding dispute resolution and commercial rules
bullets: Provides permanent institutional foundation for negotiating multilateral agreements and trade rules
Replaces unanimity with enforceable dispute settlement panels to resolve international trade friction

nodes.title: WTO Signalling Mechanism
nodes.subtitle: Institutional commitment device signaling trade orthodoxy to global lenders
bullets: Joining WTO signals adherence to free trade norms to IMF, World Bank, and credit rating agencies
Enhances sovereign credibility to attract overseas private investment and multilateral loan access

nodes.title: Agricultural Subsidies Deadlock
nodes.subtitle: Developed country farm supports restricting developing state comparative advantage
bullets: US and European Union agricultural subsidies prevent southern nations from realizing agricultural gains
Impasse over agricultural protections repeatedly stalls multilateral rounds and trade liberalization

nodes.title: Postwar Monetary Stability Order
nodes.subtitle: 1944 framework establishing dollar-pegged exchange rates and international lenders
bullets: Engineered monetary stability to prevent competitive devaluations that fueled prewar economic collapse
Created IMF and World Bank as twin multilateral pillars of global macroeconomic management

nodes.title: Bretton Woods Monetary Order
nodes.subtitle: 1944 monetary regime anchoring postwar stability via dollar-pegged exchange rates
bullets: Instituted fixed exchange rate regime tied to US dollar with multilateral balance of payments support
Established institutional mandate to foster postwar reconstruction and international financial stability

nodes.title: Dollar-Gold Anchor Standard
nodes.subtitle: US dollar as central reserve currency backed by fixed gold convertibility
bullets: US dollar functioned as primary global transaction currency anchored by 35 dollars per ounce gold peg
Central banks maintained parity margins, anchoring global liquidity until unilateral 1971 closing

nodes.title: Undemocratic Financial Governance
nodes.subtitle: Dominance of IMF and World Bank voting power by Western contributing states
bullets: United States and Western European nations hold largest voting shares and decisive executive influence
Loan conditions reflect geopolitical and commercial priorities of donors over needs of borrowers

nodes.title: IMF Crisis Stabilization Mandate
nodes.subtitle: Emergency balance-of-payments loans conditional on fiscal austerity reforms
bullets: Provides emergency liquidity to sovereign nations facing balance-of-payments and currency crises
Requires borrowers to adopt strict austerity measures, spending cuts, and free-market discipline

nodes.title: World Bank Development Mandate
nodes.subtitle: Long-term development project financing conditional on market-friendly reforms
bullets: Finances capital infrastructure and long-term development projects in developing countries
Conditions loans on recipient adoption of policies friendly to foreign investment and trade openness

nodes.title: Act III: The Finance Paradox
nodes.subtitle: Cross-Border Financial Liberalization, Mission Creep, and Capital Volatility
bullets: 1980s deregulatory push allowed financial flows to dwarf and decouple from physical trade in goods
Institutional mission creep exposed developing countries to volatile speculative capital flight

nodes.title: Financial Liberalization Doctrine
nodes.subtitle: Deregulatory policies permitting financial firms and markets to operate with minimal oversight
bullets: Eliminated cross-border capital controls and regulatory limits on financial institutions and markets
Elevated laissez-faire market self-regulation as dominant ideology governing global financial flows

nodes.title: Efficient Capital Allocation Rationale
nodes.subtitle: Theoretical doctrine that borderless capital flows to its most productive global use
bullets: Hypothesizes that unconstrained financial markets channel global savings into highest-return investments
Provided orthodox theoretical legitimacy for dismantling sovereign capital account regulations

nodes.title: Finance-Trade Divergence
nodes.subtitle: Concentration of global finance in North Atlantic detached from trade in goods
bullets: Cross-border financial transactions expanded exponentially beyond underlying volumes of goods trade
Financial assets remained heavily clustered in Wall Street and London rather than dispersing globally

nodes.title: Institutional Mission Creep
nodes.subtitle: IMF and World Bank expanding mandate from trade stabilization to capital deregulation
bullets: Institutions originally formed to stabilize trade shifted to aggressively enforcing financial openness
Prioritized interests of Western commercial banks by demanding capital account liberalization

nodes.title: Hot Money Volatility
nodes.subtitle: Rapid speculative capital inflows and sudden reversals destabilizing emerging economies
bullets: Developing markets opening to foreign finance experience volatile surges of short-term portfolio funds
Sudden speculative capital flight causes sharp currency devaluations and severe balance of payments crises

nodes.title: Emerging Market Capital Account Vulnerability
nodes.subtitle: Removal of capital controls leaving developing states vulnerable to liquidity shocks
bullets: Developing nations stripped of defensive capital controls suffer acute macroeconomic destabilization
Short-term portfolio reversals trigger systemic sovereign debt distress across recipient economies

nodes.title: Act IV: The Crisis Reckoning
nodes.subtitle: 2007-2008 Systemic Collapse, State Bailouts, and Regulatory Control Regimes
bullets: Subprime crisis demonstrated catastrophe of unchecked financial deregulation and self-regulation
Public bailouts halted systemic collapse while proving indispensability of regulatory control regimes

nodes.title: 2007-2008 Subprime Financial Crisis
nodes.subtitle: Systemic financial breakdown triggered by bank overexposure to mortgage-backed securities
bullets: Bursting of US housing bubble exposed over-leveraged, under-capitalized positions across major banks
Illiquid mortgage derivatives triggered liquidity freezes, bank failures, and worldwide recession

nodes.title: Public Bailouts and State Intervention
nodes.subtitle: Massive government rescues deployed to prevent systemic international financial collapse
bullets: Emergency sovereign bailouts and guarantees rescued large financial institutions from bankruptcy
State intervention prevented cascading contagion while revealing moral hazards of private risk socialization

nodes.title: Regulatory Control Regimes
nodes.subtitle: Prudential public supervisory frameworks indispensable for systemic economic stability
bullets: Mandates capital adequacy requirements, strict leverage limits, and asset transparency standards
Proves global finance cannot safely operate as self-regulating entity detached from public authority

nodes.title: Collapse of Market Self-Regulation Rationale
nodes.subtitle: Empirical breakdown of laissez-faire ideology in complex financialized markets
bullets: Self-regulating markets concentrated wealth and incentivized excessive risk-taking by too-big-to-fail banks
Underscored that financial liberalization is fundamentally incompatible with unmanaged risk stability

nodes.title: Bank Over-Leverage and Insolvency Failures
nodes.subtitle: Collapse of Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers from opaque mortgage exposures
bullets: Institutions carried severe leverage with inadequate capital reserves against complex mortgage securities
Counterparty credit freeze rapidly transmitted systemic distress across interconnected global banks

nodes.title: Macroprudential Governance Standards
nodes.subtitle: Post-crisis supervisory architecture reasserting sovereign state regulatory oversight
bullets: Replaces voluntary self-regulation with mandatory supervisory ratios to absorb credit contagion
Reasserts democratic state authority to ensure international financial markets serve broader society
